seoTitle: Studying in Germany: Tuition Fees, Living Costs and Funding
title: Studying in Germany: Tuition Fees, Living Costs and Funding
content:
Many German public institutions charge little or no tuition for some programmes, but studying still costs money. Check the specific course, semester contribution, living costs and visa funding evidence before making your budget.

Tuition-free does not mean cost-free

Many German public institutions charge no tuition for certain degree programmes. There are exceptions by institution, degree and location, including some programmes in Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria and many private or continuing-education courses. Read the fees page for the exact programme and applicant category.

A semester contribution is separate from tuition. It can support student services, student representation or transport arrangements. Check what the contribution includes and how often you must pay it. Do not describe a course as free while leaving out mandatory charges.

Master's study and doctoral research are different routes

For a master's, check the required previous degree, subject credits, language evidence and application method. Some universities use their own portal; others use an external application service. The route and document requirements are set by the specific course.

For a doctorate, distinguish admission from funding. You might apply for an advertised research job, a structured doctoral programme or an individually supervised project. A funded employment contract, a scholarship and an unfunded admission arrangement have different financial implications.

Make a realistic budget

Add housing, insurance, food, transport, semester contributions and initial moving costs. Research accommodation in the city where you would live. A low tuition bill does not remove the need for savings while you move, wait for your first payment or search for housing.

Applicants who need a visa must also check the accepted financial evidence. A blocked account is one possible route; a recognised scholarship or another accepted arrangement may be relevant. Use the responsible German mission's instructions before choosing a provider or transferring money.

Choose funding before relying on it

Search DAAD and university funding pages, then read the eligibility conditions for each scheme. Check which costs are covered, whether a separate admission application is needed and when funding starts. Do not count an application, nomination or possible future job as confirmed funding.

Keep a simple comparison for every course: tuition, mandatory charges, estimated living costs, funding already awarded and any remaining gap. It will show whether the programme is affordable for your situation without relying on a blanket claim that study in Germany is free.

Official information

  • DAAD: finances and tuition fees
  • German study visa information

Separate a low-fee course from a funded place

A programme charging no tuition can still require substantial living support. Before applying, record tuition, semester contributions, insurance and the costs of moving. Then check the exact scholarship or employment offer, if any. A supervisor agreeing to discuss your project is not the same as a funding commitment. Ask whether support is guaranteed, how long it lasts and what the appointment requires. Keep the official visa financial-evidence requirement separate from your personal budget: meeting a minimum requirement does not establish that your preferred city and housing plan are affordable.

Relevant listings and guides on NextApply

To see how these questions apply to a real listing, review Doctoral Position in Novel Mineral Sources for Micronutrient Deficiencies at ETH Zurich. Compare its stated requirements with your own preparation and check the official source before applying.

You can also browse ETH Zurich on NextApply and the PhD positions category. Listings and recruitment windows can change.
